stories.summary: The M50 is the busiest motorway in Ireland and experiences between ten to 20 incidents per day. Those range from the minor to the major and the Incident Support Unit is often the first on the scene. "Anything can happen," said Ryan Mulroy of the M50 Incident Response Unit. "You could be picking up debris off the hard shoulder one minute and the next minute you could be going out to a major collision on the motorway with three lanes blocked. "It's tough for everybody... Look, we have a very good crew up here and we're all colleagues... we're kind of like a big family," he said. "We all get along and we all help each other out in whatever aspect of the job as well.

stories.title: More than 650 drivers caught speeding in last 24 hours
stories.summary: A motorist driving nearly 40km/h over the speed limit was among 650 people detected speeding during the first day of a garda road safety operation. Gardaí said that since the operation began yesterday morning, 18 people were arrested for driving under the influence of drink and/or drugs. During speed checkpoints around the country, a driver was clocked at 119km/h in a 80km/h zone on the R265 at St Johnston in Co Donegal, while another was detected driving at 90km/h in a 50km/h zone on the R830 at Deansgrange in Dublin. More than 95 drivers were also detected holding a mobile phone or not wearing a seatbelt yesterday. The total number of people killed so far this year on Irish roads has risen to 153, following the deaths of a man and woman in two separate crashes this morning and yesterday. A man in his 30s died following a two-car collision in at Carrigaline in Co Cork at around 6.30am this morning, while a woman in her 70s died in a collision in Co Monaghan yesterday.

stories.title: Minister says meeting with solicitors likely next week
stories.summary: The Minister for Justice has confirmed that he has "engaged" with solicitors and that a meeting is likely next week. Speaking at the launch of One In Four's annual report, Jim O’Callaghan said letters had been exchanged. A majority of solicitors working in criminal legal aid across the country have been in dispute with Mr O'Callaghan since a new €520 flat-fee payment for legal aid cases was introduced in July. Mr O’Callaghan insists that legal aid continues to be granted by the courts; solicitors continue to provide representation, and defendants continue to receive legal services throughout the State. This week, the minister said he would meet the Law Society of Ireland regarding the dispute. In a letter to President of the Law Society of Ireland Rosemarie Loftus, Mr O'Callaghan said he had instructed his officials to "organise a meeting in the coming days to hear your viewpoint and specific concerns".

stories.title: Euro zone growth slows to 4-month low amid French turmoil
stories.summary: Growth across the euro zone's private sector slowed to its weakest pace in four months in October, driven by an energy-driven rise in costs and a renewed contraction in France amid political and financial pressures, a survey showed today. The S&P global flash euro zone Composite PMI ⁠Output Index fell to 51.9 in October from September's 53.1, its lowest reading since June and lower than all forecasts in a Reuters poll which had predicted a modest dip to 52.7. "Key to the broader slowdown is the further escalation of inflationary pressures seen during the month," said Chris Williamson, chief business economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence. "Input costs are rising sharply again, the rate of increase surging in manufacturing on the back of higher energy prices, causing firms to push selling prices higher in order to protect margins," he said. Input costs accelerated for the second consecutive month linked to higher energy, fuel and transport costs in part due to the Middle ‌East war. Despite this, firms raised their ⁠selling prices at a slower pace than in September, suggesting some margin compression. "Higher interest rates are also starting to take a toll, dampening demand, and the picture of sustained growth and stubbornly elevated inflation from the October flash PMI will likely add to further speculation of more aggressive policy tightening from the ECB," Williamson added.

stories.title: Israel demolishes homes in West Bank after fatal attack
stories.summary: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said Israel would lock down Hebron in the West Bank, go house to house and demolish homes after the Israeli military ⁠said Palestinian attackers killed two soldiers at a military checkpoint near the city. The Israeli military said it had killed two attackers, and another three soldiers had been lightly wounded in the attack. In a visit to Hebron after the attack, Mr Netanyahu said Israeli forces would enter the neighbourhood of the attackers and displace its residents. "We will evacuate the residents, we will go from house to house, we will also seize the weapons there, and all the terrorist infrastructure will be dealt with and destroyed," Netanyahu said, according to his office. "The defence minister and I are considering a very extensive IDF (army) operation in Judea and Samaria, such as has not been carried out since the Six Day War," Mr Netanyahu added, referring to the 1967 Arab-Israeli war. "The IDF is ready to execute it and we will set the timing, but it is on the way."

stories.title: County final venues a bridge between the past and future
stories.summary: In club final season, the result is pretty much the be-all and end-all. It's all about the 'who'. stories.title: Storm Boelo prompts Sunday switch for Galway final
stories.summary: An adverse weather forecast has resulted in the rescheduling of the Galway SFC final between Maigh Cuilinn and Salthill-Knocknacarra at Pearse Stadium, with the game now taking place on Sunday. With a number of weather warnings issued upon the arrival of Storm Boelo, the Galway GAA board have acted swiftly in moving the final, a repeat of last year's decider, from its original throw-in time of 7pm on Saturday to 4pm on the following day. The game will be preceded by the intermediate decider between Caherlistrane and An Spidéal at 2pm. Galway and Mayo are among seven counties which have come under a Status Orange warning from 2pm on Saturday, expiring at 9am on Sunday. The incoming threat has also prompted the Mayo board to reschedule two of their finals. Ballinrobe v Davitts in the intermediate grade will now be the curtain-raiser for Sunday's senior final featuring Castlebar Mitchels and Garrymore at Hastings Insurance MacHale Park - and will have a 1.45pm start time. The junior B final involving Ballycastle and Swinford has been moved to Bank Holiday Monday with a 1pm throw-in at the Castlebar venue.

stories.title: Iraola: Liverpool must go 'full gas' despite injuries
stories.summary: Liverpool head coach Andoni Iraola will insist his team plays "full gas" despite growing injury worries. Winger Victor Munoz missed Tuesday's Champions League win over Villarreal and was absent from training on Thursday as a result of a knock from last weekend. Iraola said his participation against Brighton on Sunday would be "difficult". Munoz makes it six players now injured and while that weakens their forward options, Iraola will not accept players trying to manage their minutes during a concentrated spell of games. "No, we cannot allow ourselves. The way we want to play you cannot play 70%," he said. "Imagine you don't have a right-winger on the bench, I will put someone as a right-winger. I prefer to do this than you save your energy so you have to last 90 minutes.

Heading into round four, Munster are the best of the provinces in ninth place, with Leinster and Ulster just behind, and Connacht back in 14th place. Plenty can change this weekend though, particularly with Leinster and Munster meeting at Aviva Stadium on Saturday evening. Ulster picked up their first win against Zebre in the Challenge Cup last week, but Richie Murphy's side are yet to win in the URC, and play the Bulls on Saturday in the first of their two games on their tour of South Africa. Connacht, who produced a brilliant win against Saracens last week, will be hoping to keep the good times rolling when they host Zebre on Friday night. Connacht v Zebre Parma (Friday, 7.45pm) is live on TG4 and Premier Sports.

stories.title: They did not go quietly - inside Ireland's last witch trial
stories.summary: It’s May 2026 and we are driving on a sunny weekday afternoon to the Islandmagee Peninsula, twenty miles north of Belfast. As the waters of Larne Lough, the body of water which separates Islandmagee from the mainland, comes into view the question arises, what do we believe really happened here on this remote spit of land back in 1711? The history books tell us that a young Presbyterian woman named Mary Dunbar was showing all the signs of demonic possession. Over a period of days, she named eight local women as witches, claiming they were responsible for her torment. The people of Islandmagee, at that time mostly Presbyterians of Scottish descent, believed Mary's accusations and the eight women were arrested, put on trial and found guilty. They are on record as fiercely protesting their innocence in court. Today the peninsula is a tourist attraction for visitors to the Gobbins, a cliff walkway suspended over the Irish Sea. Yet, there are traces of its past written into the landscape; stone built cottages clinging to hillsides, churches dating back to the 1500s, and a landmark steeped in folklore: the Witches’ Rocking Stone, a boulder overlooking Brown’s Bay.

stories.title: Sinéad O'Shea: 'You want things to be unpredictable'
stories.summary: What happens when a man born into one of America's wealthiest families uses his inheritance to support movements that oppose capitalism? Irish filmmaker Sinéad O’Shea explores that question in her new documentary, All About the Money, which follows American heir Fergie Chambers and his efforts to fund political movements aligned with his communist beliefs. "As a documentary-maker, that is exactly what you want. You want things to be unpredictable," she said. "I suppose the reason why I was so interested in the first place was that I felt like it was such a potent situation." O'Shea said there were aspects of Chambers’ character that she appreciated, particularly his willingness to speak about economic inequality. Asked whether she had warmed to him initially, she said: "Yes, there were characteristics about him that I always liked."

stories.title: Embracing the history, flavours, and spectacular views of Türkiye
stories.summary: Tara Povey experiences the crystal-clear waters, ancient ruins and delicious flavours of Türkiye. Turkey officially became Türkiye in 2022, and I didn't even notice. Despite Istanbul sitting on my travel bucket list for years, I’d never visited. I knew the trope of people going to Türkiye with receding hairlines or dodgy teeth and coming back looking like reality TV stars, but that’s as far as my knowledge went. Then, one day, after some dramatic romantic ups and downs that you may have read about, I met a kind, handsome Turkish man and suddenly I was learning about the Ottoman Empire, and how Türkiye sent aid to Ireland during the Famine. At the end of September we visited Türkiye together for the first time. We both knew my melanin-deprived skin would be no match for the Turkish heat during peak summer when temperatures reach up to 40°C. We flew direct from Dublin to Antalya with Sun Express, picked up our rental car and set off to explore the turquoise coast. Konyaalti is a stunning 7km stretch of pebbly beach with crystal-clear water and the Taurus mountains acting as a dramatic backdrop. We stayed in an apartment in Konyaalti just a few minutes' walk from the beach.

stories.title: How the French riots will affect the 2027 Elysée battle
stories.summary: The scale of last weekend's riots across France continues to bewilder. The stunned silence of around 7,000 locals, who gazed at the destroyed 19th century city hall in Limoges, has become emblematic of a broader shock at where the Fifth Republic finds itself: a democracy that seems to have lost control. Fabrice Février, director of the Media Observatory at the Jean Juarèz Foundation, said the "17 October is destined to become etched in our collective memory as a national trauma". "One of those historical dates we spontaneously mention without needing to specify the year," he added. The scenes of burning vehicles and looted Parisien boulevards have ripped into pan-European and transatlantic culture wars. Everyone from US President Donald Trump to far right leaders in Germany, Spain, Portugal and Italy have weighed in, for their own political ends, with highly partisan hot takes over what drove the violence.

stories.title: Over 100,000 fans to descend on Cork for Jazz Festival
stories.summary: Over 100,000 music fans are set to descend on Cork city for the Guinness Cork Jazz Festival this weekend. This year, the festival will feature over 500 musicians from across Ireland and the world, performing across 100 events in 80 venues. Now in its 48th year, the five-day festival is the biggest on Cork's cultural calendar and runs from Thursday to Bank Holiday Monday, 26 October The event is expected to bring in almost €45 million to the city's economy. A popular headline act this year is Luke Thomas and the Swing Cats, who are set to play two shows at the Everyman Theatre on Saturday 24 October. Mr Thomas, who described his band’s musical style as "Vintage Pop", said returning to the festival "means everything" to him.

stories.title: No measure can ease pain of scoliosis failures - minister
stories.summary: The Minister for Health has acknowledged that no measures the Government may introduce will alleviate the pain endured by those affected by failures in spina bifida and scoliosis services. She told the Dáil that stakeholders will be consulted by her officials, who will work with the Attorney General to draft terms of reference for a commission of inquiry. The minister was speaking during Statements on Children's Health Ireland (CHI), which was also attended in the visitors' gallery by some of those who have been advocating for action on the matter. Ms Carroll MacNeill said that she received the final scoping report on 9 September, and expressed her gratitude to Remy Farrell SC for his efforts to "capture the pain" and "very real frustration" of those affected. She noted that a commission of investigation, as recommended by Mr Farrell, allows for greater flexibility than a tribunal, including private hearings. She noted that witnesses can request whether to have their testimony heard in public or private.

stories.title: Lidl to invest €420m across Munster, creating 500 jobs
stories.summary: Lidl has today announced a €420m investment across Munster, which the supermarket group said will create more than 500 permanent jobs. €306m of the investment is earmarked for Co Cork, the company added. At the centre of the programme is Lidl's new €200m regional distribution centre at Little Island in Cork, alongside plans for 14 new stores across Munster and the redevelopment of 10 existing locations. As well as creating 500 jobs, including 250 in Cork, the company said the investment will also support more than 4,500 construction jobs across the 25 developments. Lidl currently employs more than 1,300 people across Munster and once the new investment is delivered, its permanent workforce in the region is expected to exceed 1,800. The €420m regional programme represents a significant part of Lidl's wider €600m five-year investment programme in Ireland, through which the retailer intends to open up to 35 additional stores around the country.

stories.title: Trump ordered to testify in BBC defamation case
stories.summary: A US judge has issued President Donald Trump a deadline to testify under oath in his $10 billion (€8.91bn) defamation lawsuit against the BBC. Judge Enjolique Lett in Miami gave the order in response to complaints by the British broadcaster that Mr Trump has refused to sit for a deposition, including cancelling a previously agreed date of 16 October. If he fails to attend the deposition by 11 December, he risks sanctions, including dismissal of his lawsuit, the court said. The US president has accused the BBC of deceptively editing its documentary 'Trump: A Second Chance' to make it seem as if he was inciting violence when he told supporters to march on the US Capitol on 6 January 2021, after losing the presidential election. The crowd proceeded to storm the US Congress in an attempt to disrupt the formal certification of Democrat Joe Biden's victory. While the BBC has apologised for the incident, which prompted the resignation of multiple senior executives, the broadcaster has denied it caused Mr Trump any real injury and moved for the case to be dismissed.

stories.summary: The Ireland women's rugby team have been ticking off new venues throughout 2026; Their eight games this year have been played across seven different stadiums, four of those hosting them for the first time. Ireland's Test with the Springbok women will be the just the second ever meeting of these sides, and the first on South African soil. With 20 years separating this game from the last meeting of the side at the 2006 World Cup, there is little in the way of history between them. And while the Springbok women aren't a powerhouse of the game like their men's side, a week in South Africa has already given the Ireland squad a sense of how passionate the nation are for the game. "It's an amazing country, very different to Ireland, with a very rich historical background," second row Dorothy Wall says. "When you come to a country, you have to pay respect to what's happened here, the culture of the people, different things like that."

stories.title: Harnedy: Hard to step away when Cork are so close
stories.summary: Cork stalwart Seamus Harnedy said it was extra-hard to step away from the county set-up because "the lads are so close" to the ultimate glory. However, the three-time All-Star made the call to retire from the inter-county game after what he described as a "tough" year in which his game-time was severely limited. The 36-year old had been battling injuries in recent seasons but was deployed as a sub in the 2025 All-Ireland final. However he wasn't introduced at any stage in this summer's All-Ireland semi-final loss to Galway, as Cork floundered in the second half. Harnedy acknowledges that in the immediate aftermath of the Galway game, this would likely be his last involvement with the Cork set-up as a player. "After the Galway game, I probably knew that was it," Harnedy told reporters ahead of the Ireland-Scotland hurling/shinty clash this weekend.

stories.title: Carrick '100%' sure he can turn United's fortunes around
stories.summary: Michael Carrick is 100% certain he can turn things around at Manchester United after the under-fire manager began his press conference with an emotional speech about the state of the club. The 45-year-old's position is hanging in the balance after Wednesday’s calamitous 4-1 Champions League loss at Como extended their winless to a seventh match in all competitions – the club’s worse run of form since 2015. Carrick will take charge of Sunday’s return to Premier League action at home to Bournemouth but there is a sense that it may only prove a stay of execution for the United head coach. But the former midfielder will not go down without a fight and began Friday’s press conference with a defiant five-minute speech, admitting "we’ve kind of lost our way a little bit" but "we’ll get it back". "There’s always conversations going on," Carrick said when he faced his first question. "I think it’s pretty obvious how we’re all feeling. "The responsibility for me to be in this position is to lead. It is my responsibility whatever goes on the pitch, what we are as a group and what we look like and what we feel like.

stories.title: Carbery starts for Leinster while Sheehan in back row
stories.summary: Joey Carbery will make his first start for Leinster in eight years, while captain Dan Sheehan has been named at number eight for their first interpro of the season at home to Munster in the Aviva Stadium on Saturday evening as the Irish provinces revealed their United Rugby Championship selections. Ireland hooker Sheehan, who scored two tries in Leinster's comfortable win in Clermont last Saturday, has intriguingly been named at number eight in the absence of Jack Conan, who picked up an injury in the act of scoring a second half try last weekend. Ronan Kelleher fills in for Sheehan in his regular berth at hooker. Carbery came off the bench as a late replacement for Sam Prendergast and has been handed his first start since his return to the province, with Prendergast ruled out due to a wrist injury suffered in training. The Irish out-half, who left Leinster in high profile circumstances in 2018, is named to start against the province where he spent six injury-riddled seasons until 2024. He is joined at half-back by Jamison Gibson-Park, who makes his first start of the season in place of Fintan Gunne, who impressed in the South African trip and made his Champions Cup debut in Clermont.

From his work with the pioneering Planxty, setting up Mulligan Records, and his long musical pairing with Christy Moore, he truly was a giant of Irish music - one who bestrode the world stage and became a beacon for those who followed. Grá Linn, located in the coastal village of Fethard-on-Sea, has become a gathering place for locals, weekend wanderers and those tracing the quieter corners of Wexford. Here you’ll find a speciality coffee culture with genuine small-town warmth, as well as great seasonal brunch dishes and pastries. Large windows frame the rhythm of village life outside, while inside the focus is on quality ingredients and thoughtful service. Whether you're fuelling up before exploring the Hook Peninsula, or returning from a sea swim at Baginbun Beach, Grá Linn is the perfect stop. Hey Darling has brought a distinctly modern energy to Kildare's coffee scene. With three branches across Sallins, Naas and Kill, this stylish coffee shop blends excellent coffee with a sharp eye for design, creating a space that feels as considered as the drinks being served.

stories.title: Have public service wages kept up with inflation?
stories.summary: Pay talks on a new public sector agreement between senior Government officials and union leaders are well under way. The workers' representatives argue wages have fallen behind due to a significant increase in inflation over recent years. For its part, the Government contends pay rises have kept pace with the cost of living from 2024 until the existing agreement expired in June of this year. The Central Statistics Office (CSO) collates figures on public sector weekly earnings before tax in the civil service, Defence Forces, An Garda Síochána, and workers in education and healthcare. Looking back over the past decade, it is clear that all categories have kept pace with inflation, but a very different picture emerges over a shorter number of years. Comparing CSO figures for the second quarter (April to June) of 2016 with the same period in 2026, civil service wages rose by 43%, Defence Forces earnings are up 50%, gardaí 40%, workers in education 39% and in healthcare 43%.

stories.title: Ballinahown in Co Westmeath named Ireland's tidiest town
stories.summary: Ballinahown in Co Westmeath has been named the overall winner of this year's Supervalu Tidy Towns competition. With a population of just 85 people, it was also named Ireland’s tidiest village. Ballinahown has a lot of young people involved in volunteering for Tidy Towns and that is what makes it such a successful committee, according to its co-chair. Speaking after the win for the village, Aoife Farrell said she was thrilled and said the Co Westmeath community is a close-knit one that takes pride in all the new amenities. "What makes Ballinahown very special - apart from all the volunteers - is our very close-knit community. stories.title: Supreme Court reserves judgment in 'super junior' appeal
stories.summary: The Supreme Court has reserved its judgment in appeals challenging the lawfulness of the presence of so-called "super junior" ministers at Cabinet. The attendance of several ministers of state at Cabinet meetings chaired by the Taoiseach is the main point of contention in appeals brought by two opposition TDs. Earlier bids by Sinn Féin Kerry TD Pa Daly and People Before Profit Dublin TD Paul Murphy challenging the practice have been unsuccessful in lower courts. Mr Murphy has argued the attendance of super junior ministers at Cabinet was inconsistent with Article 28 of the Constitution of Ireland, which says the Government "shall consist of not less than seven and not more than 15 members". Mr Daly had challenged the Government's appointment of super junior ministers on the basis that it caused issues for Cabinet confidentiality as well as an issue of expenses and allowances paid. On the third day of the Supreme Court appeal, Eileen Barrington SC, for Mr Daly, said they were arguing that any government decisions taken with the involvement of super juniors at Cabinet since 1994 - when the practice began - were unlawful.

stories.title: Mortgage drawdowns by FTB hit highest level since 2008
stories.summary: Mortgage drawdowns by first-time buyers are at the highest level since 2008, according to the mortgage drawdowns figures released by the Banking and Payment Federation Ireland. A total of 14,217 mortgages to the value of almost €4.6 billion were drawn down by borrowers in the months of July, August and September. This is a 13% increase in volume compared to the same period last year. Most of this activity was driven by first-time buyers - with 8,164 mortgages they accounted for 60% of all drawdowns in the third quarter. "Our latest figures show continued momentum across the mortgage market, with growth in drawdowns across every customer segment during the third quarter of 2026," said Brian Hayes, chief executive at BPFI. Remortgaging and switching activities saw a sharp rise as well.

stories.title: 16 dead, dozens injured in Tibet earthquake
stories.summary: China has ordered an "all-out" rescue effort in Tibet after an earthquake killed at least 16 people, injured dozens and flattened hundreds of homes, state media reported. Footage showed rescue workers with torches clambering in the dark through some of the more than 300 houses that Xinhua said collapsed in the 7.0-magnitude quake last night. Diners ran out of restaurants and items fell off wobbling supermarket shelves as the tremor struck, according to clips on state broadcaster CCTV, which said 65 people were injured. One resident told local media that her family had just gone to bed when her home shook, knocking over objects, and that they "rushed outside without even taking the time to get dressed." "My legs were shaking the entire time I was heading downstairs and by the time I reached the bottom, I was so terrified that I burst into tears," the woman said. Local residents "are afraid to return to their homes," she said. "They set up tents along the roadside or spent the night in their cars."

stories.title: O'Shea: The pride comes from representing the game
stories.summary: While the proposed resurrection of the Ireland-Australia international rules series is a fraught subject, given the current testy relations between the AFL and GAA, there is no such controversy around the annual hurling-shinty international, which takes place in SuperValu Páirc Uí Chaoimh this evening. There is little danger of Ireland's top hurlers or camogie players being lost to the bright lights and golden beaches of Oban and Inverness. In a country where the original Sky Sports mantra of "Football [soccer] first, second and third" holds true, shinty is seen as a relatively fringe pursuit, certainly by those in the big cities. The Camanachd Cup final - the game's showpiece - is televised live on BBC Alba but is generally played at venues like Bught Park in Inverness, which resembles an above average sized club ground in Ireland. The best known shinty player from an Irish perspective is Bob MacIntyre. (One thing that shinty probably shares with hurling is a high volume of low-handicap golfers at the elite end of the game.) Still, the Scots have been relatively competitive in the hurling-shinty head-to-head standings, dominating the series in the 1990s and then winning four in a row on two occasions from 2005-08 and 2016-19.
